ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Why oxygen is not definitive therapy

A child with bacterial tracheitis has improved oxygen saturation after oxygen delivery, but marked retractions and poor air movement persist. Why should the team continue urgent airway assessment despite the better saturation reading?

  1. Supplemental oxygen may improve saturation without relieving obstruction
  2. Improved saturation demonstrates that carbon dioxide clearance is normal
  3. An increased oxygen concentration reliably reduces tracheal edema
  4. Persistent retractions are expected after the obstruction has resolved
  5. Improved saturation makes subsequent complete obstruction unlikely
Answer and explanation

Supplemental oxygen may improve saturation without relieving obstruction

Supplemental oxygen may improve blood oxygenation while obstruction and ventilation failure continue to progress.

Option explanations

Supplemental oxygen may improve saturation without relieving obstruction: Supplemental oxygen may improve blood oxygenation while obstruction and ventilation failure continue to progress.

Improved saturation demonstrates that carbon dioxide clearance is normal: Pulse oximetry assesses oxygenation, not ventilation or carbon dioxide elimination.

An increased oxygen concentration reliably reduces tracheal edema: Oxygen does not directly clear the edema, exudate or secretions causing mechanical narrowing.

Persistent retractions are expected after the obstruction has resolved: Marked retractions and poor air entry indicate continuing work of breathing and possible failure.

Improved saturation makes subsequent complete obstruction unlikely: A mechanically compromised airway can deteriorate despite an initially improved saturation.
